If an AI generates thousands of novel accelerators a day but humans must manually write UVM[^fn-uvm-c01] testbenches for them, it hasn't solved the bottleneck. It has just created a catastrophic **Verification Traffic Jam**. Producing candidates faster than reviewers can check them makes that worse, so driving formal-verification tools and constrained-random testing is part of the work, not an afterthought. A generated cache controller that hides a coherence deadlock is worse than useless if the deadlock takes months to find. A working rule of thumb holds that a defect's cost grows by roughly an order of magnitude at each stage it escapes, from review to simulation to first silicon to the field, which is why a loop earns its keep by moving rejections toward the cheap end; @sec-feedback-verification-trust develops this escalation and the multi-fidelity discipline it motivates.

[^fn-zero-shot-c01]: **Zero-shot generation**: Producing a correct output for a task the model has seen no examples of, on the first attempt and without feedback. A model that cannot do this for RTL must learn through tool feedback instead, which places the slow EDA toolchain inside its training loop.

[^fn-uvm-c01]: **UVM (Universal Verification Methodology)**: The standard SystemVerilog class library teams use to build constrained-random testbenches, supplying reusable stimulus drivers, monitors, scoreboards, and coverage collectors. The testbench is often larger than the design it checks, so generating hardware faster only helps if the verification collateral scales with it.

Verification must also reach past functional correctness to hardware security. After Spectre [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre], a loop that emits hardware has to check its own structures for microarchitectural side channels, isolation-boundary violations, and hardware Trojans, which means generating the SystemVerilog assertions, security properties, and testbenches those checks require.

- @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization explains AI roles and component organization.
- @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces explains legal multi-tool action and typed feedback.
- @sec-feedback-verification-trust explains evidence, challenge, and decision relevance.
- @sec-running-the-loop shows one bounded integrated study.
- @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack shows what changes across feedback conditions and time.
- @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect examines how the field benchmarks these agents and bounds their reasoning capacity.

@sec-running-the-loop also shows how to bootstrap a study of your own, the design-loop card in @sec-architecture-20-ontology gives a compact way to inspect a completed one, and @sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist provides a reviewer's checklist.

## Open Research Questions

Every chapter in this book ends here, with the questions its argument leaves open. The sections are not a summary of what was settled. They mark where the work runs out, so a reader who wants to push on the subject knows where the edges are.

Start at the widest lens, because the opening chapter is the one place these questions can be asked before the machinery narrows them. The enterprise this book describes needs three things it does not have. It needs design data that records what failed and not only what shipped. It needs feedback fast enough that a search can learn from it, in a discipline where the honest signal takes hours. And it needs a standard that lets one group believe another group's architectural claim without rerunning it. None of the three is a modeling problem, which is why none of them is solved by a better model.


**Theme 1: The Bootstrap Data Wall.** Software models learn from millions of open pull requests and unit tests, while high-fidelity hardware data stays proprietary and closely held.

- How can a model learn foundry-calibrated physical-design behavior, such as power-delivery routing or advanced-node timing limits, without access to the proprietary PDKs that encode it?
- How far can open ecosystems like RISC-V and OpenROAD substitute for closed design data as a bootstrap corpus, and where does the gap to production silicon remain?

**Theme 2: The Missing Fast Loop.** Software agents improve fast because every attempt is graded in seconds, and hardware has no comparably fast, exact feedback loop. A loop that rejects a generator's errors cheaply is therefore worth only what it saves against a matched human-orchestrated baseline under the same budget.

- What evaluation harness could give a design loop feedback fast and exact enough to drive real learning, given that PPA, STA, DRC, and thermal checks each demand slow EDA runs?
- How cheaply can a loop catch a generator's errors, such as a hidden coherence deadlock or a microarchitectural side channel, before rejection costs more than the engineering work it was meant to save?
- How much of the verification load, including SystemVerilog assertions, security properties, and coverage models, can an AI loop produce to a standard a sign-off engineer would accept?

**Theme 3: Defining the Win.** The Lighthouse target carries an explicit stop condition, yet judging a completed run against it is itself unsettled. Novelty is the sharp edge, because a design retrieved from a memorized topology can look like a discovery, and non-obvious compositions or Pareto points outside the training distribution are only candidate ways to tell the two apart.

- When does automated search over these rugged, high-dimensional design spaces exceed what a human team could direct, rather than produce a larger set of candidates?
- How can a reviewer separate genuine architectural synthesis from a design memorized from nearby topologies [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated]?
- What would let an autonomous run from workload characterization to timing-closed layout count as a real architecture study rather than an interpolation of known baselines?

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Non-Delegable Responsibility"}
Automation can synthesize candidates, but structural integrity remains human work. The architect delineates boundaries, defines objectives, and holds ultimate accountability for physical invariants. Delegating the search does not delegate the validation.
:::


The Lighthouse prompt shows what it would take for AI to help an architect formulate, explore, implement, evaluate, explain, and defend a system design with evidence rather than settle for a plausible candidate. A defensible answer needs a clear question, meaningful alternatives, checkable artifacts, experiments, a mechanism-level explanation, and a recommendation. Readers should judge the whole body of work, not only the artifact AI produced, and ask whether its evidence supports the architectural claim.

Efficiency now couples performance, energy, power delivery, reliability, sustainability, cost, verification effort, and the time needed to obtain useful evidence. When plausible artifacts are cheap, evaluation often becomes the expensive part of the work. Search, tool feedback, interpretation, evidence, or review can each turn out to be the limiting resource.

Models and tool interfaces are changing quickly, and how far they can carry architecture work is still unsettled. What does not change is where responsibility sits. The architect frames the task, chooses abstractions, representations, and tools, sets the evidence standard, interprets the mechanisms, and remains answerable for the committed design. Keeping the inputs, results, rejections, and decisions lets others challenge the architect's work and improve it.

::: {.callout-carry-forward}
- **Carry forward:** Evaluate AI across the complete architecture work it claims to assist, and judge any demonstration by the slice of that work it actually carried. A generated artifact matters only in relation to the question, alternatives, implementation path, evaluation, explanation, and decision it advances, and a program that names no result which would show its enabling breakthrough never arrived can pursue its target for years on a premise that never holds.
- **Reader test:** Can a reader take the Lighthouse request, name the decisions and disqualifying checks each fragment implies, say which coverage or intensity check would rule out a proposed candidate before any tool runs, and name the scarce resource its efficiency claim is judged against?
- **Up next:** @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales explains why the architecture work introduced here has become harder to complete as specialization, software change, evaluation cost, and cross-layer coordination reinforce one another, and turns that explanation into a diagnostic: five ways a project stalls, and the measurements that say which one is binding yours.
:::
